meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Workers of the world, unite! You have nothing to lose but your chains'?
meta.ogDescription: The Communist Manifesto ends the other way round: chains first, then the shout. The authorised 1888 wording, and where the slogan came from.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: Marx 1818–1883 · Engels 1820–1895 · co-authors of The Communist Manifesto, 1848
answer.sourceLine: Both halves of this line come from the closing paragraph of The Communist Manifesto (1848) — but not in this shape. The authorised English translation by Samuel Moore, prepared with Engels, ends “The proletarians have nothing to lose but their chains. They have a world to win. WORKING MEN OF ALL COUNTRIES, UNITE!” — the capitals as the Project Gutenberg edition sets them (Project Gutenberg ↗), while the Marxists Internet Archive prints the same words as a title-case heading and its translator’s note states that the popular one-liner “is a popularisation of the last three sentences, and is not found in any official translation” (Marxists Internet Archive ↗).

source.heading: The passage it comes from

docMeta.dd: The Communist Manifesto (Manifest der Kommunistischen Partei)
London, February 1848 — in German, without the authors’ names
Samuel Moore, in cooperation with Friedrich Engels, 1888 — the authorised English text

source.excerpt:
The Communists disdain to conceal their views and aims. They openly declare that their ends can be attained only by the forcible overthrow of all existing social conditions. Let the ruling classes tremble at a Communistic revolution. The proletarians have nothing to lose but their chains. They have a world to win.
WORKING MEN OF ALL COUNTRIES, UNITE!
trail: The line’s two halves sit side by side in the last paragraph of Chapter IV of The Communist Manifesto, in the authorised English translation (Marxists Internet Archive ↗).
The same archive’s front matter records the translation as Samuel Moore’s, made in cooperation with Frederick Engels in 1888, of a text first published in February 1848 (marxists.org ↗).
Wikiquote records the closing passage as sourced and lists “Workers of the world, unite!” separately, as a variant translation rather than the text itself (Wikiquote ↗).
A third wording again — “Workers of all lands unite” — is what is actually carved on Marx’s tomb at Highgate Cemetery (Wikipedia ↗).
source.excerptNote: The German original reads: “Die Proletarier haben nichts in ihr zu verlieren als ihre Ketten. Sie haben eine Welt zu gewinnen. Proletarier aller Länder, vereinigt euch!” — literally “Proletarians of all countries, unite!” The familiar English slogan compresses these three sentences into one and reverses their order. The wording of the final cry is the same everywhere; only its setting varies. The capitals above are how the Project Gutenberg edition and Wikiquote print it — the Marxists Internet Archive gives the same words as a title-case heading, “Working Men of All Countries, Unite!”

author.name: Karl Marx
author.heading: About Karl Marx
author.bio: Karl Marx (5 May 1818 – 14 March 1883) was a German philosopher, social and political theorist, and revolutionary socialist who developed the theory of historical materialism and the critique of capitalism set out in Das Kapital. He did not write the Manifesto alone: he co-authored it with Friedrich Engels (1820–1895), his lifelong collaborator, who later oversaw the authorised English translation in which the famous closing cry reached English readers. The one-sentence version quoted today is the work of Marx’s readers rather than of Marx’s pen — a compression of three sentences into one.

misattribution.heading: What gets lost in the quoting
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabrication — it is a real passage that has been compressed. Three things go missing on the way to the poster.

items.who: “Workers of the world, unite! You have nothing to lose but your chains”
items.why: The Marxists Internet Archive’s note on Chapter IV states that this sentence “is a popularisation of the last three sentences, and is not found in any official translation”; the archive keeps Samuel Moore’s wording intact because Engels approved it (marxists.org ↗).

items.who: The call to unite, moved to the front
items.why: In the Manifesto the reason comes first and the cry last — “The proletarians have nothing to lose but their chains. They have a world to win. WORKING MEN OF ALL COUNTRIES, UNITE!” — and it is written in the third person, not as “you” (Wikiquote ↗).

Marx co-authored The Communist Manifesto with Friedrich Engels, and it was Engels who worked with Samuel Moore on the 1888 English translation that fixed the closing words in English (Marxists Internet Archive ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The chains and the call are both real, and both are in the last paragraph of the 1848 Manifesto — but the single sentence everyone quotes was assembled by later readers, not written by Marx or Engels (marxists.org ↗).

context.heading: Why the line mattered
lead: The Manifesto was written to order. Engels had persuaded the Communist League — which he called the first international movement of the working class — to drop the League of the Just’s old motto, “All men are brothers,” for “Working men of all countries, unite!”, and the pamphlet Marx drafted in late 1847 ends on exactly that cry (Wikipedia ↗). It was published in London in February 1848, in German, without the authors’ names on it, weeks before revolution broke across Europe.

The sentence people quote is really a slogan built out of a peroration. The Manifesto’s own order is argument first, cry last: the proletarians have nothing to lose but their chains, they have a world to win, and only then the shout in capitals. The popular version inverts that — command first, reason after — and swaps the third person for a direct “you.” That is what makes it a good banner and a bad citation.
detailsBody: On his grave. The pedestal of the tomb of Karl Marx at Highgate Cemetery in London carries a third wording again — “Workers of all lands unite” — alongside the closing line of the Theses on Feuerbach (Wikipedia ↗).

As a state motto. The slogan became the motto of the Soviet Union (“Пролетарии всех стран, соединяйтесь!”), appeared on the State Emblem, and was rendered in the language of each Soviet republic; it was also used by the Industrial Workers of the World and remains on May Day banners (Wikipedia ↗).

An earlier echo. Wikipedia’s article on the slogan notes that a similar appeal appears five years before the Manifesto, in the 1843 book The Workers’ Union by the French-Peruvian socialist Flora Tristan — a claim it sources to a 1973 article in Nineteenth-Century French Studies, which we have not read directly.
context.pull: The Manifesto puts the chains first and the shout last. The slogan does the opposite.

schema.verdictNote: Both halves are genuinely Marx and Engels. They close The Communist Manifesto (1848), co-authored by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, in Samuel Moore’s authorised English translation made with Engels in 1888. The popular one-sentence form compresses those three sentences and reverses their order, and is not found in any official translation.

sourcesVerified.claim: The closing paragraph of Chapter IV reads "...The proletarians have nothing to lose but their chains. They have a world to win. Working Men of All Countries, Unite!", and the page's translator's note states that "Workers of the World, Unite. You have nothing to lose but your chains!" is a popularisation of the last three sentences and is not found in any official translation.
The Manifesto was first published February 1848 and this English text was translated by Samuel Moore in cooperation with Frederick Engels, 1888.
The German original of the closing passage reads "Die Proletarier haben nichts in ihr zu verlieren als ihre Ketten. Sie haben eine Welt zu gewinnen. Proletarier aller Länder, vereinigt euch!"
Wikiquote's sourced entry for the Manifesto gives the final paragraph ending "WORKING MEN OF ALL COUNTRIES, UNITE!" and adds a line reading "Variant translation: Workers of the world, unite!"

The slogan is from The Communist Manifesto (1848) by Marx and Engels; the German "Proletarier aller Länder, vereinigt Euch!" literally means "Proletarians of all countries, unite!"; Engels persuaded the Communist League to change its motto from the League of the Just's "All men are brothers" to "Working men of all countries, unite!"; the slogan was the Soviet Union's state motto; and the article states that the phrase appeared five years earlier in Flora Tristan's 1843 book The Workers' Union.
The pedestal of Marx's tomb at Highgate Cemetery is inscribed with the final words of The Communist Manifesto as "Workers of all lands unite", alongside the closing line of the Theses on Feuerbach.

Project Gutenberg ebook #61 is The Communist Manifesto by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels; its plain-text file ends with "The proletarians have nothing to lose but their chains. They have a world to win. / WORKING MEN OF ALL COUNTRIES, UNITE!"
Karl Marx lived 5 May 1818 – 14 March 1883, was a German philosopher, social and political theorist and revolutionary socialist, and co-authored The Communist Manifesto (1848) with Friedrich Engels.
Friedrich Engels lived 28 November 1820 – 5 August 1895 and co-authored The Communist Manifesto (1848) with Marx.
The first edition of the Manifest der Kommunistischen Partei was published in London in February 1848 by the Office der Bildungs-Gesellschaft für Arbeiter, without the authors being named.
